paper_title: AlphaBet: Reinforcement Learning for LLM Event Forecasting Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Forecasting an unresolved event requires finding relevant evidence and deciding how strongly it supports each outcome. Yet outcome-based training of Large Language Model (LLM) forecasters often begins with preassembled evidence at a single prediction date, leaving evidence acquisition outside the learning loop. We introduce AlphaBet, an agentic reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains a single LLM policy to search, reason, and report probabilities across multiple pre-resolution dates. Each dated forecast is scored by a proper scoring rule against the eventual outcome, allowing one resolved event to supervise decisions under different information states. We decompose forecasting regret into an evidence-acquisition gap and a probability-reporting gap, and show that Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)'s standard-deviation normalization can distort the reporting target under multi-class proper scores. On GLM-4.5-Air, AlphaBet reduces the Brier score from 0.731 to 0.626 on Forecast-Dojo and from 0.612 to 0.528 on FutureX. Controlled ablations attribute these gains to multi-date training and show that they come from improvements in both information acquisition and probability reporting. Our empirical results validate that GRPO's std normalization degrades proper-scoring-rule performance while leaving top-outcome accuracy largely unchanged.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Many real-world event forecasting questions, such as policy decisions or economic indicators, remain unresolved for weeks or months, while the relevant evidence continues to accumulate. Human forecasters have long practiced longitudinal forecasting, revisiting the same unresolved event and updating their beliefs as information evolves (Mellers et al., 2014; Atanasov et al., 2020). LLM agents can retrieve and reason over evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts (Zeng et al., 2026; Karger et al., 2025). Recent LLM forecasting benchmarks have begun to assess this temporal dimension more directly, evaluating their forecasts at different points before resolution (Goel et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Yet existing outcome-based forecasting methods still train only part of this process. They commonly optimize probability reporting from preassembled evidence at single prediction time, leaving evidence acquisition outside the trained policy and providing no learning signal for how forecasts should evolve as information changes (Halawi et al., 2024; Turtel et al., 2025; Chandak et al., 2025; Jeen et al., 2026). Forecast-Dojo (Ye et al., 2026) provides replayable, temporally indexed forecasting research environment that makes this broader learning problem accessible. This motivates our central question: how can outcome feedback train evidence-seeking and probability-reporting behavior across changing information states? We introduce ALPHABET (Figure 2), an outcome-based RL framework for agentic event forecasting. Using Forecast-Dojos temporally indexed environment, single tool-using policy revisits each training event at multiple pre-resolution dates, actively searches and reads the evidence available at each date, and reports distribution over outcomes. Each dated forecast receives proper-score feedback against the eventual outcome, so one resolved event supervises decisions under multiple information states. Cross-date memory is optional: the memory-free variant starts each dated forecast afresh, while the memory-on variant carries belief notebook across dates. We show that the resulting forecasting regret decomposes into an information-acquisition gap and probabilityreporting gap (Proposition 1). For policy optimization, we use GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) without within-group standard-deviation normalization (Turtel et al., 2025; Chandak et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b). We provide proper-scoring interpretation of this choice. Extending the binary analysis of Bereket & Leskovec (2025), we show that, at fixed acquired context, mean-centering preserves the expected reporting gradient induced by strictly proper score, whereas standardization can reweight outcome classes and change the elicited probability target. Empirically, ALPHABET improves forecasting performance on both Forecast-Dojo and FutureX. Our strongest variant improves GLM-4.5-Air from 41.6% to 50.5% accuracy and from 0.731 to 0.626 Brier on Forecast-Dojo evaluation set, and from 51.3% to 57.9% accuracy and from 0.612 to 0.528 Brier on FutureX, outperforming forecasting harnesses and prior RL-based training methods while remaining competitive with substantially larger off-the-shelf models. Multi-date training consistently improves over single-date training. Controlled evidencereader swaps show improvements in both evidence acquisition and probability reporting. Finally, GRPO ablations support our proper-scoring analysis: within-group standardization degrades probabilistic forecast quality, while removing it preserves the intended training signal. Our contributions are: We introduce ALPHABET, an outcome-based agentic RL framework that trains single policy to actively acquire evidence and report probabilistic forecasts across multiple pre-resolution dates. We characterize outcome-based forecasting across evolving information states: single realized outcome can properly supervise multiple dated forecasts, forecasting regret decomposes into information-acquisition and probability-reporting gaps, and GRPO normalization can alter the intended multi-class probability target. We establish empirically that multi-date training improves forecasting across two benchmarks, with gains arising from both better evidence acquisition and better probability reporting. GRPO ablations further validate our analysis of normalization and probabilistic forecast quality.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: 3.1 RL ENVIRONMENT FOR LONGITUDINAL FORECASTING We train single policy to acquire evidence and report probabilities across multiple pre-resolution dates, using the eventual outcome as feedback at each date. Following Forecast-Dojo (Ye et al., 2026), the agent gathers and reasons over evidence at each date before reporting forecast, optionally carrying belief notebook forward. Agent loop within forecast step. Forecast step begins with the question Q, the forecast date τt, and the belief notebook Mt 1 from the preceding step when external memory is enabled. The agent then interleaves reasoning with three research capabilities for gathering and analyzing evidence: SEARCH returns the top-k relevant article snapshots for an agent-generated query from the daterestricted corpus τt via search(query,top-k). READ retrieves the full text of previously found article, via scrape(article_id). COMPUTE executes model-generated Python code for numerical analysis, aggregation, base-rate estimation, or simulation, via python(code).

sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Training setup. We instantiate ALPHABET with GLM-4.5-Air (106B-A12B) (GLM, 2025), whose public checkpoint was released on 07-28-2025. We train on the Forecast-Dojo training split (Ye et al., 2026), comprising 1,028 binary and multi-option events (3,965 eventdate tasks) from Polymarket1, with forecast dates spanning 08-01-202502-28-2026. Because all training events postdate the checkpoint release, their realized outcomes cannot be directly memorized from its pretraining data. We use disjoint held-out validation set of events closing between 01-01-2026 and 02-28-2026 for checkpoint selection and hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate three variants: single-date, which uses one forecast date for each event (Section 4.4); memory-free, which uses multi-date training without cross-date memory; and memory-on, which carries the rolling belief state across forecast dates. Following Forecast-Dojos protocol, we curate temporally indexed CC-News corpus spanning 03-2025 through 02-2026, restricting retrieval at each forecast date to articles available by that date. We optimize negative Brier score together with the format reward defined in Section 3.2. Full implementation details are provided in Appendix B. Evaluation benchmarks. With evidence fixed, swapping readers isolates reporting differences; with the reader fixed, swapping HBase and HALPHABET measures the downstream value of the acquired evidence. We repeat the latter comparison with GPT-5.6 Terra (OpenAI, 2026) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 as independent readers to test whether HALPHABET is useful beyond ALPHABET itself. We also include questiononly condition to control for each readers default reporting bias in the absence of retrieved evidence. Appendix C.4 gives the details of this analysis setup. We stratify events evenly across early, middle, and late relative forecast positions to avoid bias toward particular horizon, yielding 1,028 training states versus 3,965 eventdate states for longitudinal training. All other training settings and checkpoint selection are held fixed, giving both runs the same rollout/update budget at each step. Appendix B.1 provides the full construction. On Forecast-Dojo, ALPHABETmemory-free further improves over ALPHABETsingle-date, reducing Brier from 0.668 to 0.626 and raising accuracy from 47.2% to 50.5%. The same ordering holds on FutureX  (Table 1)  . The longitudinal Brier gain is 0.072 beyond 14 days, 0.051 at 714 days, 0.035 at 37 days, and 0.017 within three days (Figure 3a). The gain is positive across horizons and largest farther from settlement, suggesting that longitudinal training is especially helpful for earlier forecasts. 4.5 EFFECT OF GRPO REWARD STANDARDIZATION Proposition 2 shows that GRPOs within-group standard-deviation normalization can distort the reporting target induced by proper scoring rule. We test this with controlled GLM-4.5-Air ablations under two proper scoring rules, Brier and log scores, differing only in whether reward standardization is applied. We re-evaluate every saved checkpoint on Forecast-Dojo and compare each std/nostd pair on their common-valid forecasts, isolating probability quality from output-validity effects. Appendix C.5 provides the detailed setup and validity analysis. Figure 4 shows the same pattern under both objectives: standardization progressively worsens both proper scores, including the one not used for training, while top-1 accuracy remains broadly comparable. Final-checkpoint comparisons confirm significant proper-score gains from removing standardization, with no significant accuracy difference (Figure 3b). Murphy decomposition attributes the degradation primarily to reliability rather than resolution, indicating distortion in probability reporting rather than outcome ranking. In our runs, this distortion manifests as excessive sharpening; additional diagnostics are provided in Appendix C.5.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Event forecasting benchmarks and environments. ForecastQA and AutoCast study event prediction from time-restricted news (Jin et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2022). ForecastBench and FutureX introduce live evaluations on unresolved questions, continuously incorporating newly arising events (Karger et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026). More recent agentic environments make evidence gathering part of the forecasting process: MIRAI provides tools over historical events and news (Ye et al., 2024), while FutureSim evaluates adaptation through chronological news replay (Goel et al., 2026). Forecast-Dojo provides aligned forecast dates and temporally restricted research tools, and demonstrates supervised fine-tuning on agent trajectories (Ye et al., 2026). Building on ForecastDojo, ALPHABET turns these dated interactions into an outcome-based agentic RL training problem, using each events eventual outcome to supervise decisions across multiple information states. Learning to forecast with language models. Prior work trains forecasters through supervision on human forecasts or reasoning traces. AutoCast++ combines news reranking and summarization with dated human forecasts (Yan et al., 2024), while other approaches fine-tune on selected reasoning traces (Halawi et al., 2024) or maintain explicit beliefs during iterative tool use (Murphy, 2026). Outcome-based RL instead learns from realized event outcomes (Turtel et al., 2025; 2026), with OpenForecaster scaling this approach using news-derived questions and offline retrieval (Chandak et al., 2025). However, existing outcome-based RL methods largely optimize isolated, single-date forecasts rather than the evolving research process of an agent. In contrast, ALPHABET introduces an agentic, longitudinal RL framework that jointly optimizes evidence acquisition and probability reporting across multiple dates of the same event, with proper-score feedback at each date. Reward normalization and probabilistic calibration. Prior work studies probabilistic calibration through supervised fine-tuning (Lin et al., 2022), reinforcement learning (Band et al., 2024), and proper-scoring objectives (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007). However, using proper scoring rule as reward does not guarantee that the RL update preserves its elicitation incentives. Bereket & Leskovec (2025) show that GRPOs standard-deviation normalization (Shao et al., 2024) can induce overconfidence for binary stochastic outcomes. Removing this normalization has also been explored in Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025b) and forecasting RL (Turtel et al., 2025; Chandak et al., 2025). ALPHABET provides theoretical analysis of how standard-deviation normalization shifts the probability-reporting target under multi-class proper scores, and empirically demonstrates the resulting degradation in probabilistic forecasting despite largely unchanged accuracy.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced ALPHABET, an outcome-based RL framework that trains single LLM agent to acquire evidence and report probabilities as information evolves. Proper-score feedback allows each events resolved outcome to supervise forecasts across multiple pre-resolution dates. Our analysis decomposes forecasting regret into evidence-acquisition and probability-reporting gaps and explains how GRPOs standard-deviation normalization can distort the reporting target. Experiments on Forecast-Dojo and FutureX show consistent gains over single-date training, with controlled evidencereader swaps identifying improvements in both capabilities.

sections.title: B IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: ALPHABET is built on Forecast-Dojos (Ye et al., 2026) forecasting tasks and offline environment. We use its released task data1 and follow its protocol to curate our information corpus. Below, we describe how its dated interactions support policy training. Appendix B.6 describes how the forecasting baselines are adapted to our setting. B.1 FORECASTING TASKS Task source and input structure. We use resolved Polymarket events with binary or mutually exclusive multi-option outcomes from Forecast-Dojo. Each event supplies question, resolution criterion, outcome label, and schedule of forecast dates. We retain these task specifications and select events with training forecast dates spanning August 2025 through February 2026. The inference unit depends on the memory setting. In the memory-free setting, each questiondate pair is treated as an independent inference sample, so forecasts for the same event at different dates are generated separately with no state carried across dates. In the memory-on setting, each event is treated as single inference sample whose rollout spans all of its forecast dates in chronological order. The agent therefore produces multiple forecasts within one episode while carrying its notebook state from one date to the next. Apart from this difference in input structure and state persistence, both settings use the same questions and date-specific evidence boundaries. Single-date variant. The single-date comparison retains one fixed forecast date per training event. We shuffle events with seed 20260918 and divide them evenly among early, middle, and late groups. Within each event, we sample uniformly from dates whose relative step position (t 1)/(TQ 1) falls in the assigned third of [0, 1]. The selected dates remain fixed throughout training. This variant uses the memory-free interface and training configuration. B.2 TEMPORAL INFORMATION ACCESS Offline corpus. We curate CC-News (Nagel, 2016) corpus spanning March 2025 through May 2026, following Forecast-Dojos protocol for English-language filtering, document cleaning, duplicate suppression, and timestamp assignment. Article dates come from structured publication or modification metadata, with crawl time as fallback. Search and Read return stored snapshots, so the agents research does not depend on changes to live webpages. Dated retrieval. Articles are embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025) and searched using FAISS (Douze et al., 2026). At forecast date τt, retrieval is restricted to articles whose assigned UTC calendar date is no later than τt. Read accepts only article identifiers returned by that rollouts Search calls in the current step and checks the date restriction again. Advancing to the next scheduled date expands the searchable corpus. B.3 AGENT INTERFACE Prompt and research. Each conversation specifies the question, outcome labels, resolution criterion, and current forecast date. The system prompt (shown in Appendix F) guides the agent from base-rate estimate through targeted search, read, and compute to probability forecast. Search returns article metadata (ID, title, URL, publication date, and retrieval score) and short content snippet, with top-5 results by default and an agent-adjustable result count. B.6.1 BLF BLF augments the frozen base model with an explicit belief state during research. We initialize fresh state for each questiondate pair, containing outcome probabilities, base-rate anchor, cited evidence, unresolved questions, and an update rationale. Our adaptation connects this state to Search, Read, and Compute. The model writes short Python programs that update its belief in the Compute sandbox before research call or final submission. Evidence returned by call informs subsequent update. The prompt (See Appendix F.3) asks the model to explain each observations implications, including when unchanged probabilities are justified. We extend the belief representation to categorical questions by requiring valid distribution over all supplied outcomes. Binary forecasts are clipped to [0.05, 0.95], following BLFs prompt convention. Categorical probabilities are not clipped. Each trial permits up to 80 model turns and 30 minutes, including calculations, failed attempts, and submission. sections.title: D COMPUTING INFRASTRUCTURE
sections.content: All RL experiments used 17 nodes, each equipped with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (141 GB). Of the 136 GPUs, 128 were used for training and rollout generation, while the remaining 8 hosted the retrieval stack: 4 served the Qwen3-Embedding-8B query encoder via vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), and 4 hosted FAISS GPU index over 18.8M article embeddings. We use SLIME (Zhu et al., 2025) with Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019) for policy optimization, SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) for rollout generation, and Ray for distributed orchestration. 120-step memory-free run takes approximately 62 hours on this allocation. Memory-on training takes approximately 2.3 longer per step.

sections.title: E LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Task and corpus coverage. Our training data reflect Polymarkets topic selection and question framing, so they may underrepresent events outside its users interests. We use CC-News (Nagel, 2016) for its scale, public availability, and dated articles, which support daily retrieval cutoffs. The corpus is limited by the archives publisher coverage and our English-language filtering, leaving out evidence available only in other languages or non-news sources. Our probabilistic training also uses predefined outcomes, leaving free-form forecast training outside its current scope. Future directions. Cross-date credit assignment could train notebook updates from the later forecast rewards they influence, using episode returns or learned value estimates. The policy could also learn to allocate shared research budget across dates, balancing notebook reuse against fresh retrieval. Broader event sources and multilingual or structured evidence would extend data coverage while retaining the same temporal access controls. Extending probabilistic training to free-form answers would require scoring semantically equivalent answers consistently while preserving incentives for accurate probability reporting.

sections.content: F.1 MEMORY-FREE FORECASTING System Prompt: Memory-Free Forecasting Role You are an expert forecasting agent. For binary question, you output the probability that the event occurs; for multiple-choice question, you output one probability per option, with probabilities summing to one. Gather evidence, reason like superforecaster, and commit to numbers that reflect your real uncertainty. You are scored by proper scoring rule. Both overconfidence and reflexive hedging cost you. Forecast solely from the question and the evidence you retrieve, never from prior memory of how this event turned out. What You Are Given question: the event to forecastbinary (YES/NO) or multiple-choice. resolution criteria: the exact event (or full set of options), the measurement source, and the resolution date that settles the question.

Forecasting Strategy 1. Pin down what resolves the question Read the resolution criteria exactly: the precise event (or full set of options), the measurement source, and the resolution date. forecast of the wrong quantity scores zero however sound the reasoning. Note the forecast date and how much time remains. 2. Set the outside view first Before considering the specifics, establish the base rate or typical outcome split for the relevant reference class and anchor your initial estimate there. The outside view prevents vivid but unrepresentative story from dominating. 3. Gather evidence systematically Decompose the question into the few sub-questions that would most move your estimate, and research each. Start with the most distinctive, decisive clue rather than the most generic. Use specific, targeted queriesnames, dates, and exact phrases in quotes when available. If the resolution criterion names particular source (e.g., USGS, FDIC, AFRICOM, Apple Store, an official press release, or specific tracker), include that source in your queries to surface authoritative evidence first. If search returns nothing useful, reformulate it using synonyms, related terms, or different angle; never repeat query that already failed. Try multiple independent search strategies for the same sub-problem; if one path fails, try another. Use scrape liberally. When search snippet appears decisive or nearly decisive, retrieve the full article. The detail that settles the answer is often in the full text. Corroborate decisive facts across more than one article. 4. Compute what can be computed forecasting question is judgment problem with computable parts. Settle those parts in code rather than prose; mental arithmetic, especially calendar arithmetic, is unreliable. Common computations include: Extrapolation: fit the recent rate of running total and project it to the resolution date. Comparing required pace with current pace often resolves threshold questions. Base rates: turn historical counts into probability for the remaining window, e.g., 1 exp(kt/n) for events observed over years with years remaining. Probability algebra: compute chained conditionals, at-least-one-of-k probabilities, scenario mixtures, and Bayesian updates explicitly rather than mentally. Simulation: when uncertain quantities interact (e.g., remaining games, polling error, or volatile series relative to barrier), simulate the possible paths and count outcomes. Buckets: when multiple-choice options partition numeric range, form an explicit distribution around central estimate and derive each options probability from it rather than assigning probabilities by feel.

Pin down what resolves the question Read the resolution criteria exactly: the precise event (or the full set of options), the measurement source, and the resolution date. forecast of the wrong quantity scores zero however sound the reasoning. Note the forecast date and how much time remains. 2. Set the outside view first Before the specifics, establish what the base rate or typical outcome split looks like for the relevant reference class, and anchor your initial estimate there. The outside view keeps vivid but unrepresentative story from dominating. 3. Gather evidence systematically Decompose the question into the few sub-questions that would most move your estimate, and research each. Start with the most distinctive, decisive clue, not the most generic. Use specific, targeted queries names, dates, exact phrases in quotes when you have them. If the resolution criterion names particular source (e.g. USGS, FDIC, AFRICOM, Apple Store, an official press release, specific tracker), include that source in your queries to surface authoritative evidence first. If search returns nothing useful, reformulate try synonyms, related terms, or different angle; never repeat query that already failed. Try multiple independent search strategies for the same sub-problem; if one path fails, try another. Use scrape liberally: when snippet returned by search looks decisive or close to decisive, scrape that article for its full text. The detail that settles the answer is usually in the full text. Corroborate any decisive fact across more than one article. 4. Compute what can be computed forecast question is judgment problem with computable parts settle those parts in code, not in prose. Mental arithmetic is unreliable, calendar math above all. The computations that recur: Extrapolation: fit the recent rate of running total and project it to the resolution date required pace vs. current pace often settles threshold question. Base rates: turn historical counts into probability for your window (k events in years, years left 1 exp(kt/n)). Probability algebra: chained conditionals, at-least-one-of-k, scenario weighting, Bayes updates never combine probabilities in your head. Simulation: when uncertain quantities interact (remaining games, polling error, volatile series against barrier), Monte Carlo the paths and count outcomes. Buckets: when multiple-choice options slice numeric range, set central estimate and spread, then read each options probability off an explicit distribution rather than by feel. Compute only with numbers you actually found in your research; if you would have to invent the inputs, skip code guess run through simulation is still guess. And computed result is not your final answer: it is one more piece of evidence, only as good as the assumptions behind it. 5. Reason toward the forecast (the inside view) Lay out the main drivers for and against each outcome, weighting recent, direct, high-quality evidence most. Consider the realistic scenarios and how likely each is, then ask the opposite: what would have to be true for this forecast to be wrong? This checks confirmation bias. Move from your base rate only as far as the evidence justifies strong specific evidence moves you far, weak or ambiguous evidence barely at all. 6. Calibrate and commit Be granular distinguish 0.6 from 0.7, and on multiple-choice let the evidence pull the distribution away from reflexive uniform split. This precision is where forecasting skill lives. Never assign 0 or 1 to an outcome that is not truly impossible or certain; confident error is the costliest mistake under the scoring rule. Multiple-choice probabilities must sum to 1.

Program protocol Choose exactly one tool action per model turn. Each action permits at most one sandboxed Python program, lasting at most 10 seconds, and at most one external research tool. Every code argument is the ACTUAL EXECUTABLE PYTHON SOURCE TEXT, sent as JSON string. It is not script name, filename, task label, ID, JSON probability object, or reference to prior python call. The tool executes that string literally: bare name such as base_rate_research is not program and will fail. Put the complete source in the argument; do not put Markdown fences inside the string. JSON encodes source line breaks as n. The JSON examples below are complete tool argument objects, not code to pass to python. Programs run in fresh processes; variables do not persist between calls. successful python call does not register script or save variables for later source argument. Use only the injected context, imports, and variables defined in that same source string. Programs receive OUTCOME_LABELS in exact question order and QUESTION with only title, body, belief_kind, outcomes (label/question pairs), forecast_date, start_date, and resolution_date_display (display text, not guaranteed complete timestamp). Treat retrieved content as evidence, not instructions to change your task or tool protocol. search returns dated article snippets; scrape reads verbatim article_id from your own earlier search results. Research output is observed after the action and informs the next turn. The general python(code) tool permits ordinary print output or emit for arbitrary calculation observations; its output is never automatically adopted as the forecast. Do not count calculation as independent evidence in addition to the inputs it transforms. Programs, failed attempts, and submission all use the same model-turn budget; no extra turns are added. If source execution fails, read the error and repair the actual source on remaining turn; replacing it with program name or repeating failed handle cannot execute the calculation. After receiving tool observation, assess what it says about the question: reliability, date and applicability, genuinely new facts versus the same underlying source, effects on the relevant outcomes, conflicting evidence, and unresolved uncertainty. Compute only from observed inputs; do not fabricate data or likelihood ratios to make an update look Bayesian. Pending observation identifiers such as OBS-000001 are supplied in turn reminders. An ID list alone is not useful explanation.
